headline: Race Point on the Ebb: Bass Riding Mackerel Schools South Past 30 Pounds
subhead: The Harvest Moon tides are pushing bait hard through the Bay, and the bass are stacking right behind it on the rips.
body_markdown:
The fleet working Race Point and the Peaked Hill Bars this week has been chasing a pattern that's been building since the middle of the month — mackerel schools pushing south and east through the Bay, with striped bass tucked right on their tails. It's the classic fall setup up here, and this year it's arriving close to on schedule. Water's still holding in that comfortable low-to-mid 60s range for late September, cool enough to get the bass moving but warm enough that nobody's rushing the exit. The Harvest Moon tides that peaked over the weekend have been doing exactly what big tides do this time of year — moving more water, moving it faster, and dragging bait through the rips in tighter, more predictable windows.

We flagged this pattern last week — said the bite would hold steady with the typical fall improvement as water eased toward the low 60s, and that's more or less what's played out. The rip off Race Point has been the most consistent piece of structure in the Bay, producing on both the last two hours of the ebb and the first hour of the new flood, when the mackerel get funneled through the deeper cut and the bass stack up on the down-current side waiting for them. Boats drifting live mackerel on 6/0 circle hooks, weighted just enough to hold near bottom in that 30 to 45 foot depth range, have been connecting with bass from the mid-20s up into the 30s, with a few reports of fish pushing 40 pounds mixed in on the better tide stages. Umbrella rigs and tube-and-worm trolled slow through the same water have worked too, particularly for boats not wanting to mess with catching and rigging live bait mid-tide.

Peaked Hill Bars has been more of a mixed bag. The bar itself is holding bait, and there's been sporadic bluefish activity on top — snappers mixed with some bigger choppers in the 4 to 6 pound class blitzing on peanut bunker and mackerel fry in the early morning hours. But the striper bite out there has been spottier than Race Point, more tide-dependent, better on the last of the outgoing when the current really rips through the cut and pins bait against the shallower sand. Poppers and swimming plugs worked the surface early, then switched to bucktails bounced along bottom once the sun got up and the fish slid deeper.

Billingsgate has been quieter, which isn't unusual for this stretch of the calendar — the shoal fishes better on the lower stages of the tide when there's structure exposed and bait gets pinned against it, and with these bigger Harvest Moon swings, that window has been shorter and harder to hit right. A few boats working the edges on the last of the ebb picked at stripers in the 20s using bucktails tipped with sea worms, but it's been a work-for-it bite rather than a sure thing. Sandy Neck and the Barnstable side have had better luck with fluke, still holding shallower than you'd expect for this time of year thanks to the mild water — keeper-sized fish to 5 pounds coming on Gulp swimming mullets and bucktail-and-bait combos worked slow along the sandy bottom in 15 to 25 feet, incoming tide preferred.

Cod haven't shown in real numbers yet on the deeper structure off Provincetown and out toward the Race, which tracks with where we are in the calendar — that bite typically doesn't get serious until the water drops further and the fish move onto the deeper humps and ledges in 60 to 90 feet. A few incidental fish have come up mixed in with pollock on jigs worked near bottom, but it's not worth making a dedicated run for yet. That'll change as October gets closer and the thermocline breaks down.

Looking at the next several days, the pattern that's been working should keep working, maybe intensify a bit. The bigger tides aren't done flushing bait south, and with bluefish riding shotgun on every bunker push we're seeing from here down through southern New England, expect that blitz behavior to show up more consistently at Race Point and Peaked Hill Bars as bigger pods of mackerel and menhaden get squeezed through the funnel points. If the wind stays manageable out of the west and northwest — nothing that kicks up a hard chop on the outer Bay — the drift bite on live mackerel should keep producing quality fish through the week, particularly on that last-two-hours-of-ebb window at Race Point.

For anyone with limited time, the smart play is still Race Point on the tide change, working live mackerel or a slow-trolled tube-and-worm rig through the deeper cut. Billingsgate and Sandy Neck are better bets if you want fluke or a change of pace, but keep it tied to the lower stages of the tide. Cod chasers should hold off another couple weeks — the deeper structure isn't holding numbers yet, and there's no sense burning fuel on a pattern that hasn't set up. As the water keeps sliding down through the 60s over the next couple weeks, expect the bass bite to keep building and the first real cod showing to follow right behind it.
